entry: City in [[Tamil Nadu]] state, southern India, on the Noyyal River and the second-largest city in the state after Chennai. Coimbatore was ruled successively by the Cheras, the medieval Cholas, the [[Vijayanagara Empire]] and the Nayaks, and in the later 18th century it came under the Kingdom of Mysore. After the defeat of [[Tipu Sultan]] in the Anglo-Mysore Wars, the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] annexed it to the Madras Presidency in 1799. The city became the capital of a new district in 1804. After independence it grew into an industrial centre, exporting jewellery, wet grinders, poultry and auto components. Its textile industry gave it the nickname "Manchester of South India." The Coimbatore Wet Grinder and Kovai Cora Cotton are recognised as Geographical Indications by the [[Government of India]].

Small, flat, usually round piece of metal, most often issued by a government as money. Coins are standardized in weight and produced in large quantities at a mint to facilitate trade. The earliest coins date from the late 7th century BC in [[Lydia]], in Anatolia, and were made of [[Electrum|electrum]], a natural alloy of gold and silver. Most modern coins are made of base metals, and their value comes from their status as fiat [[Money|money]] established by law. Coins usually last far longer than banknotes, which last about four years, compared with 30 years for a coin. Bullion coins of copper, silver or gold, intended for collectors and investors, are an exception to the rule that a coin's face value is higher than its metal content.

Grey, hard, porous fuel with a high carbon content, made by heating [[Coal|coal]] or petroleum in the absence of air. Coke is used mainly in smelting [[Iron ore|iron ore]] and also as fuel in stoves and forges. Industrial coking takes place in ovens at usually around 1,000–1,100 °C (1,800–2,000 °F), driving off volatile products such as coal tar and ammonia. Petroleum coke is a similar product obtained from crude petroleum in refineries.

Genus of about 160 species of perennial flowering plants, native to West Asia, Europe, the Mediterranean coast and East and southern Africa. The genus, first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753, grows from bulb-like corms and produces crocus-like flowers in late summer or autumn, before its strap-like leaves appear in spring. Common names include autumn crocus, meadow saffron and naked lady. All species are toxic, and the plants contain the [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] colchicine. Colchicine is used pharmaceutically to treat [[Gout|gout]] and familial Mediterranean fever, and temperate species are grown in gardens as ornamentals.

Hypothetical [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] reaction occurring at or near room temperature. In 1989 electrochemists Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons of the University of Utah reported excess heat from the [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]] of [[Heavy water|heavy water]] on a [[Palladium|palladium]] electrode, which they attributed to nuclear processes. Expectations faded as replication attempts failed, and the U.S. Department of Energy declined to fund cold fusion after reviews in 1989 and 2004. A small community of researchers continues the work under the names low-energy nuclear reactions (LENR) or condensed matter nuclear science (CMNS).

British rock band formed in London. Its members are vocalist and pianist Chris Martin, guitarist Jonny Buckland, bassist Guy Berryman and drummer Will Champion. The debut album *Parachutes* (2000) included the single "Yellow." *Viva la Vida or Death and All His Friends* (2008) won a [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Best Rock Album. The band has sold over 170 million records worldwide, and its *Music of the Spheres* World Tour became the first by a band to gross $1 billion.

Irish actor. Farrell made his breakthrough in [[Steven Spielberg]]'s science fiction film *Minority Report* (2002), after his first lead role in the war drama *Tigerland* (2000). He won a Golden Globe Award for *In Bruges* (2008), a dark comedy made with frequent collaborator [[Martin McDonagh]]. For *The Banshees of Inisherin* (2022) he won a Volpi Cup and a second Golden Globe Award, and he received an Academy Award nomination. He played the Penguin in *The Batman* (2022) and in the [[HBO]] miniseries *The Penguin* (2024), which earned him a Golden Globe Award.

English actor and producer. Firth was identified with the "Brit Pack" of young British actors in the mid-1980s. His portrayal of Mr. Darcy in the [[BBC]] adaptation of [[Jane Austen]]'s *Pride and Prejudice* brought him stardom. He won an Academy Award for Best Actor for playing [[George VI|King George VI]] in *The King's Speech* (2010), and a BAFTA Award and Volpi Cup for *A Single Man* (2009). Later films include *Love Actually* (2003) and *Kingsman: The Secret Service* (2014). In 2012 he founded the production company Raindog Films.

American Army general and diplomat. Powell served as the 65th U.S. secretary of state from 2001 to 2005, the first Black American to hold the office. As chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff from 1989 to 1993, he oversaw 28 crises, including the invasion of Panama and Operation Desert Storm in the [[Gulf War]]. He formulated the Powell Doctrine, which limits American military action unless it meets criteria for national security interests, overwhelming force and public support. As secretary of state he presented the rationale for the Iraq War to the [[United Nations Security Council|United Nations Security Council]], a speech he later admitted contained substantial inaccuracies.

Technique of art production using an assembly of different forms to create a new whole, usually by gluing flat pieces onto a flat surface. The term derives from the French *coller*, "to glue." Collage may incorporate newspaper clippings, ribbons, paint, [[Paper|paper]] scraps, photographs and other found objects; assemblage is the three-dimensional equivalent. Paper collage is first known from 10th-century Japan. The technique reappeared as an art form in the early 20th century, when [[Pablo Picasso|Pablo Picasso]] and Georges Braque coined the term *papier collé* as collage became a distinctive part of modern art. In the 18th century Mary Delany created 985 botanical collages, which she called flower Mosaicks.

Group of loose-leafed cultivars of *Brassica oleracea*, the species that includes [[Cabbage|cabbage]] and [[Broccoli|broccoli]]. Collard is part of the Acephala, or "[[Kale|kale]]," group and is classified as the variety *Brassica oleracea* var. *viridis*. It is grown as a food crop for its large, dark-green, edible leaves, which are cooked and eaten as a [[Vegetable|vegetable]]. Collard has been cultivated as food since [[Classical antiquity]]. The biennial plant has an upright stalk, and its leaves are tastier and more nutritious in cold months, after the first frost. After [[World War II]], as people moved to towns, the number of varieties commonly grown in the United States fell to five, although seed savers preserved many others.

Unsolved problem in mathematics concerning repeated arithmetic operations on positive integers. The conjecture holds that repeatedly halving even numbers and replacing odd numbers with three times the number plus one always eventually reaches 1. It has been shown to hold for all positive integers up to 2.36×10²¹, but no general proof has been found. The problem is named after the mathematician Lothar Collatz, who introduced it in 1937. Efforts to solve it have produced new techniques and many partial results.

[[Hobby]] of seeking, acquiring, organizing and displaying items of interest. Collections are most often of manufactured goods such as [[Coin|coins]], stamps and art, but they may also consist of natural objects such as birds' eggs, butterflies, rocks and seashells. Some collectors gather broadly, while completists try to acquire every item in a defined set. Antiques are generally at least 100 years old. Older collectables too young to be antiques, such as [[Art Deco]] and [[Art Nouveau]] pieces, are called vintage. Items that were once everyday objects but are now collectable because almost all examples have been discarded are called ephemera. The value of a collectable is set on the secondary market, and a price guide lists typical selling prices.

Form of agricultural production in which multiple farmers run their holdings as a joint enterprise. There are two broad types: agricultural cooperatives, in which members farm jointly, and state farms, which are owned and run by a centralized government. The aggregation of farmland is called collectivization. Under the [[Aztec Empire]], land in central Mexico was held by calpulli, which granted families the right to farm parts of it. The [[Haudenosaunee]] redistributed land among households every few years. In the [[Soviet Union]], [[Joseph Stalin|Joseph Stalin]]'s collectivization drive, launched in 1929, encompassed over 97 percent of peasant households by 1940. It was followed by the 1932–1933 famine, which killed 6–7 million people in Ukraine alone. In China, the [[Great Leap Forward]] established people's communes from 1958 to 1961, and the [[Great Chinese Famine]] that followed starved approximately 30 million people.

Educational institution offering secondary, vocational or higher education. In the [[United States]], a college usually offers undergraduate programs, either as an independent institution or as the undergraduate program of a [[University|university]], and the word is often used as a synonym for university. Community colleges provide affordable education, usually limited to two-year associate degrees. The word derives from the [[Latin]] *collegium*, a body or guild in ancient Rome. [[Eton College]] was founded in 1440 by letters patent of King Henry VI. Colleges in [[Belgium]], France and [[Switzerland]] provide [[Secondary education|secondary education]].

Mixture of microscopically dispersed insoluble particles suspended throughout another substance. A colloid has a dispersed phase, the suspended particles, and a continuous phase, the medium of suspension. The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry describes its particles as having at least one dimension roughly between 1 nanometre and 1 micrometre. Colloids are classified by phase as [[Emulsion|emulsions]], [[Foam|foams]], [[Aerosol|aerosols]] and sols, and examples include [[Milk|milk]], [[Fog|fog]] and [[Mayonnaise|mayonnaise]]. Some colloids are translucent because of the Tyndall effect, the scattering of light by the particles. The field was expanded by [[Michael Faraday]] and Thomas Graham, who coined the term colloid in 1861.

City on the [[Rhine]] River, the largest in the German state of [[North Rhine-Westphalia|North Rhine-Westphalia]] and the fourth-most populous in [[Germany]]. It has over one million inhabitants and is part of the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Founded in Germanic Ubii territory in the 1st century AD as the Roman *Colonia Agrippina*, Cologne was the capital of the Roman province of Germania Inferior. During the Middle Ages it was a free imperial city of the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and a major member of the [[Hanseatic League]]. Heavily bombed in [[World War II]], the city saw its population fall by 93%, mainly due to evacuation, and around 80% of its historic city centre was destroyed. Its landmarks include the [[Cologne Cathedral]], and [[Lufthansa]], Europe's largest airline, has its main corporate headquarters in the city.

[[Gothic architecture|Gothic]] Catholic cathedral in [[Cologne]], Germany, and seat of the Archbishop of Cologne. Construction began in 1248, was halted around 1560, and was completed to its original medieval plan in 1880. At 157 m (515 ft), it is the tallest cathedral in the world and the tallest twin-spired church. It was planned to house the reliquary of the Three Kings and was declared a [[World Heritage Site]] in 1996. It is Germany's most visited landmark, attracting an average of 6 million people a year.

Largest city and executive and judicial capital of [[Sri Lanka]], on the island's west coast. Colombo is also the island's financial centre and a tourist destination, and it is the administrative capital of the Western Province. The metropolitan area has an estimated population of 5.6 million, and 752,993 people live within the municipal limits. Colombo became the capital when Sri Lanka was ceded to the [[British Empire]] in 1815, retaining that status at independence in 1948. Administrative functions later moved to Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, and Colombo became the commercial capital. The Portuguese began to build a fort there in 1517, and the [[Port|port]] of Colombo is a key transshipment point in [[South Asia]].

American businessman and founder of [[KFC|Kentucky Fried Chicken]]. Sanders held jobs as a steam engine stoker, insurance salesman and [[Filling station|filling station]] operator before selling fried chicken from a roadside restaurant in North Corbin, [[Kentucky]], during the [[Great Depression]]. He developed a "secret recipe" and began franchising in 1952, when the first franchise opened in Utah. In 1964 he sold the company for US$2 million to investors led by John Y. Brown Jr. and Jack C. Massey. He then became a salaried brand ambassador, and his image remains a symbol of the company.

Process of sending people to live in and govern another country, sometimes used synonymously with settlement. Settler colonialism is a type in which settlers themselves enforce control while maintaining a connection with their metropolitan country, often by assimilating, oppressing, displacing or killing the existing inhabitants. Ancient city-states of [[Phoenicia|Phoenician]] and Greek origin founded colonies around the Mediterranean, and the [[Roman Empire]] conquered much of western Europe, North Africa and West Asia. Many European cities, including [[Cologne]] and [[London]], began as Roman colonies. In the Middle Ages, the [[Franks]], [[Anglo-Saxons]] and [[Vikings]] established new settlements across Europe. European colonization of Australia, New Zealand and Oceania was fueled by explorers who regarded the land as terra nullius, or "nobody's land." Mexico's 1824 General Colonization Law and the United States' [[Manifest destiny|manifest destiny]] doctrine furthered colonization.

Decreased ability to see color or differences in color, ranging from mostly unnoticeable to total absence of color perception. It is usually an inherited, sex-linked condition. The most common form is congenital red–green color blindness, which affects up to 1 in 12 males (8%) and 1 in 200 females (0.5%), and is more common in males because the responsible opsin genes lie on the X chromosome. Rarer genetic causes include blue–yellow color blindness and achromatopsia. Damage to the [[Eye|eye]], optic nerve or [[Brain|brain]], medication and old age can also reduce [[Color vision|color vision]]. There is no cure for most causes. Depending on the jurisdiction, color blind people may be ineligible to become aircraft pilots, train drivers, police officers or firefighters.

Property of a light source, defined by comparison with the color of light emitted by an idealized black body. It is expressed in [[Kelvin|kelvins]] (K) and used in [[Lighting|lighting]], [[Photography|photography]], videography and publishing. Light sources that do not emit thermal radiation, such as fluorescent lamps and LEDs, are assigned a correlated color temperature. The [[Sun]]'s effective temperature is 5,772 K, and the color temperature of sunlight above the atmosphere is about 5,900 K.

Historical body of knowledge describing the behavior of colors in mixing, contrast, harmony and symbolism. It dates back at least to [[Aristotle]]'s treatise *On Colors*, and Bharata's *Nāṭya Shāstra* contains an early functional theory of color. Its formalization began in the 18th century, within a controversy over [[Isaac Newton]]'s theory of color, published in *Opticks* (1704). Traditional color theory tends to be subjective and artistic, while color science is more objective and has functional applications in chemistry, astronomy and color reproduction. The two diverged by the end of the 19th century, although they have intertwined throughout history.

Ability to perceive differences between light of different frequencies independently of its intensity. Color perception begins when photoreceptors in the eye respond differently to incoming light, and the signals pass through many layers of neurons to the brain. The visible spectrum ranges from about 380 to 740 nanometers, and the human eye can distinguish up to a few hundred hues. Color vision is found in many [[Animal|animals]]; in [[Primate|primates]] it may have evolved under selective pressure for foraging for young leaves, ripe fruit and flowers. The trichromatic theory, proposed by [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] and [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], describes human color vision based on three types of cone cells. Variations in cone function cause [[Color blindness|color blindness]].
